extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of poetry criticism; literary critics and close-readers
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and evaluative criteria for judging lyric/sonnet poetry: technical prosody (metre, rhythm, rhyme), diction and imagery, sincerity and emotional authenticity, and the relation of sound to sense. Draws on reader protocols and examples to illustrate strengths and faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity, simplicity, probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Merits of sincerity, of simplicity, of probability. Provides clear picture of subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer expression that seems genuinely felt and straightforward rather than affected. Example praise: lines that 'tremble' with feeling or reach Wordsworthian heights; criticism when endings or vocabulary weaken sincerity (e.g. last stanza weak, 'As live words will' called 'very feeble').

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction must fit subject and effect; avoid pompous, ridiculous, or inappropriate word-choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific anti-patterns: phrases like 'vaporous vitiate air' or grandiloquent 'prognostications' may be damning; 'poetic diction' used merely to sound poetic is counted against the writer. Choose words with precise, defensible function in the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and consistency of imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Images should be coherent, logically compatible, and consistent across the poem (no sudden incompatible shifts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticisms include contradictory or confusing images (e.g. 'arrased distance' vs 'dim with flowers'; monument/effigy vs dust imagery; unexplained 'slaves' at head/feet). Incoherent imagery jars the reader and undermines the poem's credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and movement
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem's rhythm (movement of lines) should express and reinforce the emotion and subject; rolling/sonorous rhythms can create grandeur, while skittish or 'brisk' rhythms can be intolerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise where 'rhythm at once suggests real emotion' or 'the roll of the lines is as the rumble of heavy clouds.' Criticize 'briskness, almost the skittishness' or rhythms that make the poem feel like a 'jazz tune' only tolerable a few times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and avoidance of verbosity/ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: An economy of expression — lack of verbosity or ornamentation — is often appropriate, especially for weighty subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise for 'an economy, a lack of verbosity' that is 'utterly appropriate to the subject.' Anti-patterns: licentious verbosity where words are used for their 'mothy aura' rather than meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre and versification (scansion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrical regularity, natural stress patterns, and proper scansion are technical criteria; irregular arrangement or harsh scansion can spoil effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of faults: ugly accent placement ('the' stressed), lines that require forced elisions, irregular stanzaic syllable counts, or deranged metre in the final stanza. Prosodic correctness should feel natural and suit the poem's tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of style and tone to the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's style and tone must be appropriate to the poem's occasion and subject (e.g. elegy should be restrained and dignified).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise: 'restrained and yet dignified, fresh without false emphasis, sincere without gush.' Criticism: 'stilted and high-flung style' or frivolous tone for solemn subjects (e.g. tripping rhythm with solemn theme).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of simile and metaphor with purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Similes and metaphors should clarify or deepen the reader's perception, not merely decorate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good example: similes that 'make the shades of experience clearer.' Bad examples: metaphors that are 'absurd' or 'nonsense' (e.g. 'wise imaginations of the mantel of a cloud'), or images introduced without explanatory force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance (or justified use) of pathetic fallacy/personification
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributing human feelings/actions to nature or objects is open to objection unless there is good reason or advantage in the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many complaints (clouds having 'desires', mantles having 'imaginations', milk 'smiling') rest on assuming such attributions cannot occur; the text's guidance: they are permissible if justified by the poem's purpose, but unjustified personification invites criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and avoidance of mere imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem should offer fresh treatment and not simply ape a well-known manner (e.g. Shelley) or rely on worn phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words 'so well worn as to have become commonplace unless very adroitly used' are suspect. Imitation or derivative manner that yields inconspicuous success is criticized as lack of originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding stock responses and facile appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems that exploit familiar 'stock' experiences risk eliciting pre-formed reader responses that mask real reading and can provoke rejection or lazy reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Danger: readers may substitute a known poem or stock response and either heap abuse or fail to read closely. Poets should aim to give new significance beyond commonplace themes and avoid inviting merely automatic emotional reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional authenticity versus sentimentality/sermonizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine emotion and contemplation are praiseworthy; mawkishness, maudlin tone, or pulpit-like sermonizing are faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of faults: 'this gush of sentiment and evangelical piety', 'maudlin', 'a sermon in four stanzas.' A poem should avoid cheap sentimentality and have an underlying value to the emotion it expresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony of sound with sense (sonority reinforcing meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem's sounds (sonority, long words, sparing syllables) should help convey the poem's ideas and mood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good cases: 'sound so well suited to its sense', 'sonorous lines' that set one dreaming. Bad cases: prose-like language in blank verse where sound fails to support the sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural unity, balance and appropriateness of form
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem should be an 'harmonious whole' with fitting sentences, balanced movement, and an appropriate rhyme-form or stanzaic plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise for pieces where 'every sentence seems fitting' and the rhyme-form is of 'considerable subtlety.' Criticism where stanzaic irregularities, poor arrangement, or imbalance produce confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of syntax and referents
rubrics_metrics.description: Grammatical clarity — clear antecedents and unambiguous referents — is necessary for readers to follow meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: it
rubrics_metrics.description: Might I be permitted to ask what "it" refers to? ... '
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguity over what a pronoun or phrase refers to (e.g. whether 'it' refers to Christian charity or to something else) makes the poem muddled and harder to read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding contradictory imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid contradictions within images or between image and description (e.g., 'arrased distance' implying clarity vs 'dim with flowers').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such contradictions ('arras shows clear-cut figures' vs 'dim with flowers') indicate carelessness or confusion in image-management and invite reader objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader engagement vs swoon-reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the poem demands active analytical work or merely induces a passive 'swoon' in the reader is a criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text questions the critical value of poems that allow 'swoon-reading' (readers 'loll at ease' and produce private poems) versus those that invite close analysis; poems that seduce without rewarding scrutiny may be less valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's experiential depth as basis for value
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet who writes from lived experience produces more convincing values and judgments than one who relies on second-hand knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique: work that seems produced 'at second hand' without the writer's own experiences often lacks authority and conviction.
